name: Balbriggan Martello Tower
blurb: Tower number twelve of the chain, put up in 1805 to guard the pier below.

lore.title: Built on a Danish fort
lore.body: Raised in 1805 as number twelve in the chain begun the year before under Colonel Benjamin Fisher of the Royal Engineers, and armed with a single twenty four pounder. A manuscript of 1804 records that it was built on part of an old Danish fort. Photographs from 1929 show it still carrying its parapet, render, flagstaff and chimney. The parapet was later taken down, and the stone is said to have gone into houses on Drogheda Street.

name: Red Island Martello Tower
blurb: A tower that has been a barracks, a coal depot, tearooms and a holiday camp.

lore.title: From gunners to tearooms
lore.body: Number eleven in the chain, set on Red Island to cover the landing places at Skerries and watching its twin out on Shenick Island. Royal Artillery gunners held it until it was disarmed in 1874, and after that it went through a run of lives that no ordnance board foresaw: a private residence, a coal depot, tearooms, and finally the focal point of a holiday camp from the nineteen fifties to the early seventies.

name: Shenick Island Martello Tower
blurb: The island tower off Skerries, still holding its iron shot furnace and gun rails.

lore.title: Rainwater to the tank below
lore.body: Number ten in the chain, built at the north end of the island in limestone under rough lime render, with granite for the gun platform on the roof. The platform floor was laid on an incline and grooved so that rain ran down into a tank in the basement, which is how the garrison drank. It still holds its iron shot furnace, gun rails and iron rings. Twelve troops were stationed here in 1857.

name: Drumanagh Martello Tower
blurb: A tower dropped inside an Iron Age promontory fort, later used against smugglers.

lore.title: Sold to a general for fifty pounds
lore.body: Number nine in the chain, planted in the eastern quadrant of a much older coastal promontory fort, with sunken roadways running from the earlier defences to its door. In 1821 it was handed to the Preventive Water Guard and turned on smugglers rather than on the French. Twelve troops occupied it in 1857, it was disarmed by 1874, and in 1908 the War Department sold it to General Palmer for fifty pounds.

name: Balcarrick Martello Tower
blurb: Tower number six, standing at the water's edge where Donabate beach runs out.

lore.title: Rented, then bought outright
lore.body: Number six in the chain, at the end of Balcarrick Road by the water at the north end of Donabate beach. Building began in 1804 under Colonel Benjamin Fisher and every Dublin tower was armed and finished by December 1805, each with one twenty four pounder. The Royal Artillery kept it until at least 1830. John King rented it from 1896 and bought it outright in 1909.

name: Robswalls Martello Tower
blurb: Known locally as Hick's Tower, with a galleon weather vane on the roof.

lore.title: Hick's Tower
lore.body: Number five in the chain, set landward of the Coast Road southeast of Malahide, covering the harbour mouth and the strand. Disarmed and leased to Baron Talbot by 1897, then sold off by the War Department in 1908. It is known locally as Hick's Tower after Frederick George Hicks, who turned it into an Arts and Crafts house with a conical roof and brick casing, and set on it a bronze weather vane of a full rigged galleon by the McLoughlin ironworks.

name: Carrickhill Martello Tower
blurb: The tower above Velvet Strand, now carved up into four flats.

lore.title: Manned by one invalid gunner
lore.body: Number four in the chain, north of Velvet Strand at Portmarnock. For most of its working life it was held not by a garrison but by a single invalid gunner of the Royal Artillery. It was disarmed by 1874 and sold in 1928 for conversion to living accommodation, gaining an upper storey, a crenellated parapet, a bay window and a north wing. It now holds four apartments between the road and the sea.

name: Ireland's Eye Martello Tower
blurb: The only two gun tower of the chain, out on the island off Howth.

lore.title: The two gun tower
lore.body: Number three in the chain and the odd one out. Every other tower north of Dublin carried a single twenty four pounder; this one was built as a two gun tower, the largest in north county Dublin, set on a rock outcrop at the island's north west end to command the anchorage and the approaches to Howth. It is well preserved and is the only one that still holds all its original Board of Ordnance boundary stones of 1805.

name: Lusk Round Tower
blurb: A round tower absorbed as one corner of a later four cornered belfry.

lore.title: One tower of four
lore.body: The round tower stands in St Macullin's graveyard and now serves as the detached north east turret of the fifteenth century belfry beside it, so the early Christian tower and the medieval one read as a single building with four corners. It is coursed limestone, eight floors under a conical roof, about thirty four metres high, the wall tapering from 1.4m to 0.9m. The conical cap was restored in 1860 by William Reeves, rector of Lusk.

name: Swords Round Tower
blurb: Four storeys of early tower with a plain Latin cross stuck on the top.

lore.title: A rebuilt head
lore.body: The tower belongs to the monastic enclosure that Swords grew around. It rises four storeys, about twenty six metres, entered on the east through a lintelled doorway with inclined jambs, and is lit by plain square headed openings above the door and at the same level north and south. A corbelled roof covers the first floor with timber floors above. The upper part is a later rebuild, finished off with an undecorated Latin cross.

name: Clondalkin Round Tower
blurb: The only complete round tower in Dublin, and it survived a powder mill blast.

lore.title: It outlived the powder mill
lore.body: St Mochua, also called Cronan, founded the monastery here in the seventh century. Vikings raided in 833 and Olaf the White, first Norwegian king of Dublin, set a fort on the place; the monastery burned in 1077. The tower is coursed calp limestone, twenty six metres tall, walls under a metre thick, with a lintelled doorway high in the east face. A powder mill nearby later blew up and the tower, remarkably, survived.

name: Finglas High Cross
blurb: A granite cross moved up from Watery Lane and set at the graveyard gate in 1806.

lore.title: Brought up from Watery Lane
lore.body: The cross has stood at the entrance to the graveyard only since 1806; before that it lay at Watery Lane. It is ringed granite, 2.16m high and 1.55m across. The east face carries two raised ribs forming the outer ring, with the outline of a cross in relief and a roundel at the centre. There is decoration on the arms and shaft, animal forms and spirals on the north side, and a cross and ring in high relief on the west.

name: Kilgobbin Cross
blurb: A one armed granite cross whose base is an old bullaun boulder.

lore.title: Christ in a long robe
lore.body: National Monument number 226 stands thirty metres north west of Kilgobbin church, a ringed granite cross that has lost its southern arm. Both faces carry a carved Christ, the Crucifixion on the east and on the west what may be the Risen Christ or Christ in Glory. The shaft tapers downward into a rounded boulder that already held a bullaun. It belongs with the Cashel and Moone crosses, the group in which Christ wears a long robe.

name: Tully Crosses
blurb: Two granite crosses standing in the fields near the ruin of Tully church.

lore.title: A stone roof with shingles carved on it
lore.body: The taller cross, 2.34m of plain granite with a ringed head, is tenth or eleventh century and stands about a hundred metres north west of Tully church. Its capstone is cut in the shape of a house and the carver went to the trouble of showing shingles on the roof. It was reset into a cube shaped base after 1860. The second cross, 2.2m high, shows a figure in a full length garment holding a crozier.

name: Broome Bridge
blurb: The bridge where a mathematician cut his formula into the stone in 1843.

lore.title: Quaternions, carved in passing
lore.body: The bridge takes its name from William Broome, a director of the Royal Canal Company. On the sixteenth of October 1843 William Rowan Hamilton was walking the towpath here when the algebra of quaternions came to him, and rather than lose it he cut the formula into the bridge. The original scratching is long gone, but the bridge is still the place mathematicians come to stand.

name: George's Dock
blurb: A dock named for a king who came to open it and then did not turn up.

lore.title: The king who did not arrive
lore.body: The stone dock was designed by John Rennie and named after George IV, who travelled to Ireland in 1821 for the express purpose of opening it. He failed to turn up. Lord Castlecoote opened it instead, and the name stuck to the king who had not come. The inner dock north of it carries the same story.

name: George's Dock Bridges
blurb: A pair of bridges that rolled backwards on curved rockers to let ships in.

lore.title: The Chicago rocker
lore.body: These are bascule bridges of the rolling lift type, supplied by Sir William Arrol and Company of Glasgow, the firm established in 1873. The mechanism is not Scottish but American: it was invented by the Chicago engineer William Donald Scherzer, who died in 1893 at thirty five, and patented that same year by the Scherzer Rolling Lift Bridge Company. Rather than swing, the span rolls back on a curved rocker.

name: Famine
blurb: Six thin bronze figures walking the quay towards the emigrant ships.

lore.title: Walking to the ferry port
lore.body: The group of bronze figures on Custom House Quay commemorates the famine of the eighteen forties. The elongated profiles, the tattered clothes and the gaunt faces are meant to carry the desperation of the hundreds of thousands who walked along this stretch of river front to the ferry port. The sculpture stands on the ground they crossed rather than in a square set aside for it.

name: Fishamble Street Music Hall
blurb: Where Handel's Messiah was sung for the first time, six months after opening.

lore.title: First performance of the Messiah
lore.body: The hall on Fishamble Street is best known for one evening. The first performance anywhere of Handel's Messiah was given here in 1742, just six months after the hall itself had opened. The building that carried one of the most performed works in European music was therefore barely half a year old, and the composer was in the room.

name: Smock Alley Theatre
blurb: A theatre inside a church built on the site of an older theatre.

lore.title: Theatre, whiskey store, church, theatre
lore.body: The former church of Saints Michael and John was designed by the architect John Taylor and raised on the site of the Theatre Royal of Smock Alley, which Michael Willis had designed in 1735. The playhouse closed in 1787 and the building was put to work as a whiskey store before the church went up. A theatre company has since taken the church back.

name: Sunlight Chambers
blurb: An office block with the history of soap modelled in coloured tiles outside.

lore.title: A frieze advertising soap
lore.body: Lever Brothers built this for themselves to designs by Edward Ould, an English architect who had worked at Port Sunlight, the firm's model village on Merseyside. The two bands of coloured faience running round the front tell the history of making and using soap, which is to say they advertise the owner's trade. They were modelled by the English sculptor and potter Conrad Dressler in his Buckinghamshire studio.

name: Phoenix Park
blurb: A royal deer park of the 1660s that the public was let into in 1747.

lore.title: Laid out for deer, not for people
lore.body: The park was laid out in the middle and later seventeenth century as a royal deer park, commissioned by the viceroy James Butler, Duke of Ormonde. It was not made for the city at all. Lord Chesterfield opened it to the public in 1747, and it is reputedly the largest enclosed urban park in Europe. The deer are still there, descended from the original herd.

name: Grand Canal Graving Docks
blurb: Deep water docks built in 1796 that ships could rarely get into.

lore.title: Built too small for the ships
lore.body: Grand Canal Dock was designed by William Jessop and opened in 1796, completing the canal all the way from the Shannon to the Liffey. Three graving docks were cut here for building and repairing ships. It did not work: the sea locks were too small and the Dodder silted the entrance, so vessels often simply stayed at the Liffey quays. The southernmost dock closed in 1851 and became a coal yard.

name: The Bull Wall
blurb: A wall proposed by Captain Bligh that accidentally made an island.

lore.title: Bligh of the Bounty, surveying Dublin Bay
lore.body: The northern wall was proposed in 1801 by Captain William Bligh, the same Bligh who had been set adrift from the Bounty twelve years earlier and who was then surveying Dublin Bay. George Halpin, the City Engineer, approved the plans. The wall was built to scour the bar at the harbour mouth, and the sand it trapped instead piled up behind it and became Bull Island.

name: Howth Road Milestone
blurb: A stone counting the miles to the mail packet port at Howth.

lore.title: Telford's road to the packet
lore.body: The stone marks the distance to the port at Howth, which mattered because Howth was the mail packet station and the road carried the London post. Thomas Telford was contracted in the early nineteenth century to improve the Howth Road for exactly that traffic. The milestone is a survivor of the engineering programme that tied Dublin to the crossing at Holyhead.

name: Saint John the Baptist, Drumcondra
blurb: Two friends share one grave here, and one grave is caged against robbers.

lore.title: Gandon and Grose, in the same grave
lore.body: The church was built in 1743 with money from Mary Coghill in memory of her brother Marmaduke, on the site of the medieval Priory of All Saints. The graveyard holds the architect James Gandon and the antiquarian Francis Grose, who were friends and are buried together in one grave, along with Patrick Heeney, who composed the national anthem. The caged grave at the north east corner is there because of body snatchers.

name: Drumcondra House
blurb: A house by the architect of Parliament, with a dark story in its grounds.

lore.title: Hangings in the grounds after 1798
lore.body: The original house is believed to have been designed by Edward Lovett Pearce, who also built the Irish Houses of Parliament. Its first occupant was Marmaduke Coghill, who entered Trinity College at fourteen and went on to be Judge of the Prerogative Court and Chancellor of the Exchequer. Insurgents of the United Irishmen are thought to have been hanged in the grounds after the rebellion of 1798.

name: All Hallows Folly
blurb: A tiny mock temple by a Florentine architect, now facing a graveyard.

lore.title: A Florentine in Drumcondra
lore.body: This small classical temple was built in the second decade of the eighteenth century as a folly on the lands of Drumcondra House, and it was designed by the Florentine architect Alessandro Galilei, who is better known for the front of San Giovanni in Laterano in Rome. It now serves a graveyard holding some fifty five memorials, among them the grave of John Hand, who founded All Hallows College.

name: Clonturk House
blurb: Its garden wall used to be part of O'Connell Bridge.

lore.title: A bridge in the garden
lore.body: The balustrade dividing the garden from the house was once part of the superstructure of O'Connell Bridge, taken down during works there and re-erected here. Early on there was an attempt to turn the grounds into pleasure gardens to rival Vauxhall in London, which came to nothing. From 1955 to 2009 the Rosminian Order ran it as a school for the blind, and cared here for Thomas Dudley, the Dublin street character known as Bang Bang.

name: Hampton Convent
blurb: Once the home of the first secretary of the Bank of Ireland.

lore.title: From bank to cloister
lore.body: The complex was formerly Hampton Lodge, and in the late eighteenth century it was the home of Thomas Williams, first secretary of the Bank of Ireland, and his wife Mary Ann. The Carmelite Sisters bought it in 1858 and extended it a long way westward, keeping to the same manner, so that the house of a banking official disappeared into the middle of a convent.

name: North Dublin Union Auxiliary Workhouse
blurb: An auxiliary workhouse, run by nuns since 1892 and still in use.

lore.title: The overflow workhouse
lore.body: This was built as the Auxiliary Workhouse of the North Dublin Union, the building the Union put up when the main house could not hold the numbers coming through its doors. The Daughters of Charity have run the site since 1892, and it has stayed in institutional use ever since under the name Saint Vincent's, so the workhouse never became a ruin or a museum.

name: Baymount Castle
blurb: Granby Hall, then a bishop's lease, then a castle, then a fire.

lore.title: Four names in a hundred years
lore.body: The house began as Granby Hall, and in 1775 the lease was taken by Doctor James Traill, Bishop of Down and Connor. It was renamed Baymount Castle in 1838, burned in 1851, and in 1898 the lease passed to Lord Ardilaun of the Guinness family. It now serves as a Jesuit retreat house under the name Manresa, its fifth identity.

name: Clontarf Road Postbox
blurb: A Victorian postbox still standing in a state that replaced her.

lore.title: Dated by the maker's mark
lore.body: The box carries the cipher VR for Queen Victoria, and the maker's mark of W.T. Allen of London dates it to between 1887 and 1901. Boxes of this kind were not removed after independence but repainted green and kept in service, so a walker on the seafront is posting letters into a piece of nineteenth century British street furniture that simply changed colour.

name: Saorstat Postbox, Drumcondra
blurb: A postbox stamped for a state that existed for only fifteen years.

lore.title: Fifteen years of insignia
lore.body: The insignia on this cast iron box references Saorstat Eireann, which dates it precisely to the brief life of the Irish Free State between 1922 and 1937. A new government with very little money still went to the trouble of casting its own postboxes, and the box is one of the small ways the state announced that it now existed.

name: Seventh Lock, Royal Canal
blurb: A late 1700s lock sitting directly under a Victorian railway bridge.

lore.title: Two transport ages, one spot
lore.body: The lock dates from the late eighteenth century, built when the Royal Canal was the fast way to move goods across the middle of Ireland. A railway bridge of the mid nineteenth century now crosses directly above it. The two structures sit in the same few metres of ground, the second of them built by the industry that put the first out of business.

name: Saint Maelruain's Church
blurb: A spiked Gothic church keeping the name of the monk who started Tallaght.

lore.title: The Martyrology of Tallaght
lore.body: The dedication preserves Maelruain, who founded the early Christian monastery at Tallaght where the Martyrology of Tallaght was written. That monastery stood on another site, beside the present priory, but this church kept the name and also kept the tower of the medieval parish church that preceded it. John Semple designed the rest, and its emphatically spiked roofline sets it apart from the ordinary run of First Fruits churches.

name: Saint Mary's Priory
blurb: A Victorian priory that swallowed the archbishops' medieval country house.

lore.title: Built around what was already there
lore.body: The priory stands on the site of the medieval country residence of the Archbishops of Dublin, and parts of that earlier building were absorbed into the present one rather than cleared away. J.J. McCarthy designed the complex, which is characteristic of nineteenth century institutional architecture in Ireland, and it has given Tallaght a centre through every stage of the town's growth around it.

name: Oldbawn Bridge
blurb: A single arch over the Dodder, widened so carefully you cannot see the join.

lore.title: Copied exactly, twice
lore.body: This sturdy single arch bridge is one of a family of Dodder bridges widened to take modern traffic. The interesting part is the workmanship of the widening: the west and east elevations were copied with such exactness that the later half reads as the original. It is best appreciated from the riverbank rather than from the road that crosses it.

name: Rathfarnham Graveyard
blurb: A graveyard that changed religion in the eighteenth century and kept the graves.

lore.title: It changed hands, the dead stayed
lore.body: The site has medieval fabric and a rich history of its own: it was Roman Catholic and became Church of Ireland during the eighteenth century, keeping everyone already buried in it. Among the finely carved gravestones are those of the Shaw and Yelverton families, so a single enclosure carries both the older burials and the memorials of the families who took the parish over.

name: Rathfarnham Church
blurb: Its stained glass remembers the Shaw and Stoker families of the parish.

lore.title: Windows to the Shaws and the Stokers
lore.body: The church is a building of several phases, the serene classical proportions of the early work sitting under later Gothic additions. Its windows are the thing to look for: there is stained glass here commemorating the Shaw family and the Stoker family, two names that recur in the parish and in nineteenth century Dublin far beyond it.

name: Rathfarnham Dovecote
blurb: A pigeon house left stranded when the castle demesne around it vanished.

lore.title: Evidence of a demesne that has gone
lore.body: A bold, simple structure that keeps its original form and much of its material. It once stood inside the grounds of Rathfarnham Castle, and it is now one of the clearest pieces of evidence left of how far that demesne reached and what went on inside it. Dovecotes were working buildings, kept for meat and eggs through the winter.

name: Rathfarnham Courthouse
blurb: A courthouse built almost at the scale of a house.

lore.title: Justice at domestic scale
lore.body: This is a restrained and pleasantly detailed courthouse, and what marks it out is how small it is: almost domestic in scale, closer to a large house than to the civic piles put up for the same purpose elsewhere. It shows an early stage in how courthouse design developed, and it is an important piece of local history as well as of the street.

name: Fairview Oil Mills
blurb: Ruined mill walls standing up above the treeline in a public park.

lore.title: Industry left standing in parkland
lore.body: The mill is ruinous, but the walls stand proud of the tree line and impose a historic character on the parkland that now surrounds them. It is a good example of functional industrial architecture and an important reminder that Clondalkin was an industrial place before it was a suburb, which is easy to forget walking the park today.

name: Lucan Weir
blurb: A weir cut partly out of the riverbed itself, and the last trace of a mill.

lore.title: The mill it served has gone
lore.body: An unusual weir of the late eighteenth century, formed partly out of the bedrock of the river rather than built up entirely from cut stone. It almost certainly served a mill on the north bank, and it is now the last remnant of it. The mill has disappeared completely; the thing that fed it is still working the water.

name: Rathcoole Glebe House
blurb: Built as a charter school, later a dwelling, later the rectory.

lore.title: Charter school, house, rectory
lore.body: The building started life as a charter school, part of the eighteenth century network of schools set up to educate the poor of Ireland in the established religion. It did not stay one. It passed afterwards into use as a private dwelling and then as the rectory of the parish, and the three uses are all legible in a single building on the edge of the village.

name: Rathcoole Library
blurb: The old Court of Petty Sessions, now lending books instead.

lore.title: Petty sessions on Main Street
lore.body: This was the Court of Petty Sessions for Rathcoole, the lowest rung of the court system, where local magistrates dealt with drunkenness, trespass and small debt. It is a prominent landmark on Main Street with a gable front and pedimented doorway, typical of such buildings in the early twentieth century, and it has been particularly well maintained since becoming the village library.

name: Rathcoole National School
blurb: A symmetrical village school with the teacher's house set just beside it.

lore.title: The school and the master's house
lore.body: A well executed design that once stood as a socially important building for the people of Rathcoole, with gables to the front elevation and flanking doors giving it a handsome symmetry. It was built as a pair with the national school teacher's house to the south west, which is the detail worth noticing: the master lived on the job, next door to the classroom.

name: Drumanagh Promontory Fort
blurb: A headland cut off by three banks, with Spanish oil jars in the ground.

lore.title: Roman pottery on an Irish headland
lore.body: A defended headland some three hundred and fifty metres long, cut off by three closely spaced banks with ditches in front of them. Excavations between 2018 and 2022 found Iron Age deposits, human remains dated to the centuries either side of the birth of Christ, and evidence for textile production. They also found almost eighty sherds of Dressel 20 oil jars from the Roman province of Baetica in southern Spain.

name: Howth Portal Tomb
blurb: A five metre roofstone resting on its portals above a collapsed chamber.

lore.title: The roof outlasted the room
lore.body: The tomb stands by a path under tree cover at the edge of the Deer Park golf course, at the foot of Muck Rock on the north side of Howth Head. The chamber is small, a little over two and a half metres long, and it has collapsed. The roofstone has not: it measures 5.2m by 4.2m and nearly two metres thick, and it still rests on the edges of the two portal stones.

name: Brenanstown Portal Tomb
blurb: A granite capstone the size of a room, wedged in a steep sided glen.

lore.title: Drainage cut into the roof
lore.body: A national monument in state care, set down in a steep sided glen. The granite roofstone is 5.1m by 4.5m and 1.75m thick, wedge shaped, resting on two portal stones and three sidestones over a chamber and an antechamber. Two depressions worked into the top of the roofstone are thought to have been cut to carry water off it, which suggests the builders expected it to stand a long time.

name: Taylorsgrange Portal Tomb
blurb: Three granite uprights left of four, the fourth broken about 1876.

lore.title: An iron furnace among the burials
lore.body: Three tall granite orthostats form three sides of a chamber opening south south east; the fourth stone was broken around 1876. Excavation between 1984 and 1987 found an oval cairn with charcoal and cremated bone, and a later pit burial holding an upturned Food Vessel over a cremation. The same ground gave up a Late Neolithic and Early Bronze Age assemblage and, much later, an Iron Age bowl furnace.

name: Woodtown Portal Tomb
blurb: A drawing of 1781 shows stones here that are no longer there.

lore.title: What the 1781 drawing shows
lore.body: A single chambered tomb facing north west, its massive granite roofstone 6.3m long and over three metres wide, now resting on a broken portal. A second portal stone lies nearby. The reason to look carefully is a drawing made in 1781 which shows further stones standing at the monument that are not there now, so the tomb has lost fabric within recorded memory.

name: The Shed Stone
blurb: A tomb at the head of Glenasmole that locals simply call the Shed Stone.

lore.title: Named for what it looks like
lore.body: The tomb sits on the north bank of a stream at the head of the Glenasmole valley and is known locally as the Shed Stone, a name that records what generations of people working this ground thought it resembled rather than what it is. It is a small chamber built of two granite portals and a backstone, carrying a capstone 2.1m long.

name: Kilmashogue Wedge Tomb
blurb: A wedge tomb reused much later for three cists of cremated bone.

lore.title: Reopened by later people
lore.body: A gallery tomb about six metres long, divided into a main chamber and an antechamber and set inside three lines of orthostats that give it its wedge shape. Only the northern part of the cairn survives. Later people came back to it: three cists were inserted holding food vessels and cremated bone, along with a fireplace filled with charcoal. It is a national monument in state ownership.

name: Ballyedmonduff Wedge Tomb
blurb: A heel shaped cairn on Two Rock Mountain with its kerbstones still set.

lore.title: Beaker pottery by the hundred sherds
lore.body: A wedge tomb inside a heel shaped cairn on Two Rock Mountain, its gallery running east to west in three parts: antechamber, main chamber and an end chamber at the east. Twenty five original kerbstones survive, set close together, with complex revetting behind them. Excavation produced more than a hundred and fifty sherds of Bell Beaker pottery, neolithic fragments, flints and a polished hammerstone.

name: Dunsoghly Castle
blurb: The one Irish tower house that still has its original medieval roof timbers.

lore.title: The roof nobody replaced
lore.body: A late fifteenth century tower house of the Plunkett family, four storeys with a turret at each corner, built of coursed limestone with dressed quoins and a battered base. The ground floor is barrel vaulted and the marks of the wicker centring used to turn the vault are still visible in it. What makes it exceptional is at the third floor, where substantial original roof timbers survive, along with Tudor chimneys and battlements.

name: Malahide Castle
blurb: One family held this for eight hundred years, minus twelve.

lore.title: Out for twelve years, back for three hundred
lore.body: The Talbots received these lands from Henry II in 1174 and held the castle until 1973, an unbroken run apart from one interruption: in 1653 Miles Corbet took possession, and the family were not restored until 1665. A late medieval core sits inside heavy rebuilding of around 1760 in Georgian Gothic. The Oak Room holds corbel heads of Edward the Fourth, sixteenth century panelling and a Flemish carving of the Assumption.

name: Stella's Castle
blurb: A tower in a tillage field with a murder hole over an off centre door.

lore.title: A hemp yard and a haggard
lore.body: Known locally as Stella's castle, a three storey tower standing in a tillage field. An Inquisition of 1541 lists what stood around it: a threshing house, a hemp yard and a haggard, which is a working farm rather than a fortress. By the Civil Survey of 1654 to 1656 it was simply an old castle belonging to the parsonage of Portrane. The doorway is unusually set off centre and covered by a murder hole.

name: Lanistown Castle
blurb: A stepped battlement tower left alone in the grounds of a Georgian house.

lore.title: Cleared away around 1820
lore.body: A three storey tower house with stepped battlements and an angle tower at the south west, standing in the grounds of Newbridge House. A spiral stair in the south west corner leads to corbelled chambers, and an attached building on the east had a mural passage running to a garderobe. Extensive buildings once stood to the north and east of it; they were demolished around 1820 when the demesne was tidied up.

name: Donabate Church Tower
blurb: A three storey living tower built onto the side of the parish church.

lore.title: The priest lived in the fortification
lore.body: A residential tower attached to Saint Patrick's Church, rising three storeys to a stepped battlemented parapet and entered through a pointed arched doorway with chamfered jambs on the north. The first floor has a wall press and a fireplace. It is a reminder that in the late medieval Pale a parish priest might need somewhere defensible to sleep, and built it onto the church itself.

name: Balrothery Tower House
blurb: The minister's castle, with a blocked arch and the scar of a lost house.

lore.title: Held by the minister of the parish
lore.body: A three storey rectangular tower of coursed limestone with dressed quoins, a spiral stair, and a machicolation on the north wall for dropping things on anyone at the base. A pointed arched doorway on the west, now blocked, once led into a vaulted ground floor. The Civil Survey of 1654 to 1656 identifies it as the castle held by the minister of Balrothery. A gabled building was attached to it and has left its scar.

name: Kilsallaghan Castle
blurb: A castle fought over in 1642, now one surviving west end in a paddock.

lore.title: Byrne against Coote, 1642
lore.body: The castle stands in a low paddock south of Kilsallaghan church and saw a major engagement in 1642 between Royalists under Lieutenant General Byrne and Parliamentarians under Sir Charles Coote. Only the west end survives, with a turret at the south west and a stair turret at the north west. The vaulted chamber at the south west of the ground floor still shows the wickerwork centring used to build it.

name: Saint Margaret's Well
blurb: A tepid well enclosed as a bath, that people came to for their health.

lore.title: Lime, soda and sulphur
lore.body: A plaque on the tank says Sir John Plunkett of Dunsoghly, who died in 1582, walled the spring in to make a bath. People came here for their health rather than only for devotion: D'Alton wrote in 1838 that the water held lime, muriate of soda, nitrate of kali and sulphur, and that it bubbled up constantly tepid. The well began to dry about twenty years ago and the base is now grassed over.

name: Biddy Boughy's Well
blurb: A well said to have moved house after a woman washed clothes in it.

lore.title: The woman who drove the well away
lore.body: Marked simply as Holy Well on the Ordnance Survey six inch map of 1837, and reached by a lane off the old road through Balrothery. The local name carries the story: a woman called Biddy Boughy is said to have polluted it by washing clothes in it, whereupon the well dried up and broke out again elsewhere in the village. It was described in 1958 as a good well of clear water and was uncovered again by enthusiasts in March 2014.

name: Saint Michael's Well, Grallagh
blurb: A vaulted well house in a graveyard, with a shamrock cut on the first step.

lore.title: Three steps down, and a pattern in August
lore.body: The well sits in the south quadrant of Grallagh graveyard under a stone building, three steps down to the water beneath a vaulted roof, with a shamrock carved on the first step. The map of 1837 calls it Saint Michael's Well; locally it has also been Saint Macullin's and Saint Patrick's. The water was held to cure whooping cough, sore eyes and rheumatism, and the pattern day fell on the first Sunday in August.

name: Sandycove Martello Tower
blurb: The granite tower over Scotsman's Bay where Ulysses opens.

lore.title: Numbered one to sixteen, but only fourteen built
lore.body: A granite tower over Scotsman's Bay, begun in 1804 under Colonel Benjamin Fisher and finished by December 1805. The southern chain has an oddity in its bookkeeping: the towers and batteries south of Dublin are numbered from one to sixteen, but only fourteen towers were ever built. Its battery held five twenty four pounders and two ten inch mortars. It is better known now as Joyce's Tower, from the opening of Ulysses.

name: Dalkey Island Martello Tower
blurb: A larger than standard tower whose guns could reach a mile over Killiney Bay.

lore.title: A mile of solid shot over the bay
lore.body: Tower number nine stands on the highest point at the south end of Dalkey Island, built of dressed granite with its entrance facing north towards the mainland. It is larger than the other towers and has no machicolation, and it carried two twenty four pounders on a circular platform. The battery beside it worked three guns on iron rails, firing generally southwards over Killiney Bay; solid shot carried somewhat over a mile.

name: Dalkey Signal Tower
blurb: One of eighty stations built to flag a French invasion, abandoned by 1815.

lore.title: Eighty towers watching for the French
lore.body: A square signal tower of about 1804 to 1805, two storeys over a partial basement, built of coursed rubble and granite with its doorway at first floor level, now blocked. It was part of a system of more than eighty signal stations put up by the British Board of Ordnance to pass warning of a French invasion around the coast. The invasion never came and the network was abandoned by the middle of the eighteen tens.

name: Tara Hill Tower and Battery
blurb: Tower and three gun battery together, 250 feet above the sea at Killiney.

lore.title: Tower and battery, still as a pair
lore.body: Number seven of the southern chain, set two hundred and fifty feet above sea level east of Killiney Hill Road. Most of the chain has lost one half or the other; here both the tower and its three gun battery of twenty four pounders survive together. A single storey building is attached at the rear of the battery, reaching the tower's first floor through a vertical recess cut in the thickness of the wall.

name: Howth Castle
blurb: A gatehouse joined by a battlemented wall to a tower house with corner towers.

lore.title: Four centuries welded together
lore.body: The castle stands on the north side of Howth Head looking out to Ireland's Eye. A gatehouse is joined by a battlemented wall to a massive three storey tower house with towers at its corners, and a two storey hall of the seventeenth century adjoins it on the east. Classical alterations followed in the early eighteenth century under William St Lawrence. Carved architectural fragments from earlier phases are built into the structures around it.

name: Goat's Castle, Dalkey
blurb: A fortified merchant's store whose first floor became the town council chamber.

lore.title: Drawn by Beranger in 1765
lore.body: Goat's Castle stands at the junction of Castle Street and White's Villas, a rectangular granite tower of three storeys with a vaulted ground floor and a stair tower projecting to the south east. A drawing made by Gabriel Beranger in 1765 records staircases and entrances that have since gone; the present south entrance is later. The first floor, panelled in wood and over ten metres long, served as the council chamber of the town.

name: Swords Castle
blurb: Not a castle but an archbishop's walled manor house of about 1200.

lore.title: A manor, not a fortress
lore.body: Built about 1200 as the manorial residence of the Archbishop of Dublin, on rising ground at the north east end of the village. The curtain wall encloses roughly one and a third acres, with the entrance on the south. Inside are a chapel with a residential tower, three storeys over a vaulted ground floor with a trefoil headed window, and an oratory that keeps its medieval tile pavement. Excavation found a rock cut ditch suggesting an outer moat, and burials older than the gatehouse.

name: Castleknock Castle
blurb: A polygonal keep on a motte, besieged by Edward Bruce in 1316.

lore.title: Bruce came up this hill
lore.body: A polygonal keep with a curtain wall stands at the east end of the motte, now two storeys. Sir Hugh Tyrell built it about 1174, and Edward Bruce besieged it in 1316 during the Scottish invasion of Ireland. A sketch of 1698 shows it still four storeys high with battlements, so most of its loss is recent rather than medieval. The enclosed ground inside the walls is used as a cemetery.

name: Belgard Castle
blurb: A tower house corner absorbed into a Georgian mansion on a low hill.

lore.title: A castle hiding inside a house
lore.body: The north west angle of a tower house is built into an eighteenth century mansion on the slope of a low hill, so the older building survives as one corner of the newer one. It was associated with the Talbot family from the fifteenth to the seventeenth century. It rises three storeys, of tightly coursed masonry with dressed quoins and lit by slit loops, and the battlements on top are an eighteenth century addition.

name: The Roman Tower
blurb: A viewing tower copied from a Roman tomb in Provence, then moved.

lore.title: Copied from a tomb in Saint Remy
lore.body: The tower was a viewing platform over Dublin Bay and an eye catcher in the grounds, its design apparently based on the Tomb of the Julii at Saint Remy in France. It began as part of the roofscape of the house. Benjamin Lee Guinness and his brother Arthur bought the Thornhill estate in 1835 and renamed it Saint Anne's after the holy well above the Naniken river; Lord Ardilaun moved the tower to where it stands in 1873.

name: Bettyglen
blurb: An Arts and Crafts house built for a Jameson, looking out over Bull Island.

lore.title: Built for the distiller's view
lore.body: The house was built in the early twentieth century to designs by F.G. Hicks for George Jameson of the Jameson Distillery in the city centre. It is Arts and Crafts work, with an irregular plan, a variety of openings and a deliberate mixing of materials. It was set high on purpose: the site overlooks Bull Island, and when it was built it commanded that view without obstruction.

name: Manor House Gateway
blurb: Granite piers reused from a house the Howth family built in the 1600s.

lore.title: Piers older than the gate they hold
lore.body: These rusticated granite piers were probably taken from an earlier entrance to Bettyville, the house that stood on this site, which the Howth family built in the late seventeenth century. Later in the nineteenth century it was occupied by Richard Kelly, a wealthy Catholic merchant who gave a three part stained glass window to Saint Assam's church when it was built in 1864. The house came down in 1957.

name: Raheny Milestone
blurb: One of a series counting from the GPO to the mail boat at Howth.

lore.title: Measured from the GPO
lore.body: A subtle reminder of nineteenth century civic organisation. The stone is one of a series that marked the distance between the General Post Office in the city centre and the port and mail station at Howth, so the whole road was measured from the counter where the letters were handed in. Thomas Telford was contracted early in that century to improve the Howth Road and speed the mail along it.

name: Walmer Villa
blurb: A dower house with an open ironwork veranda, built beside its parent house.

lore.title: The house for the widow
lore.body: Walmer was built as a dower house for Belmont next door, the house a widow moved into so the heir could take the main house. Belmont is now a Capuchin friary. Walmer was later occupied by the Moore family, relations of the Earls of Drogheda, who added a bedroom wing to the west. Its elegant open work cast iron veranda is of technical as well as artistic interest.

name: The Bacon Curer's House
blurb: Turned back to front in the last century, probably when it was a hotel.

lore.title: Ham, bacon, lard and the navy
lore.body: In 1862 this was listed as the residence of Edward McVey, described as a ham and bacon curer, lard refiner, navy contractor and general merchant, who worked out of premises on Mabbot Street in the city. The house was reoriented in the twentieth century, probably when it became a hotel, so the original front now faces away from the road and the old rear is the entrance.

name: Enniscorthy Postbox, Raheny
blurb: A rare Irish cast postbox, most of its neighbours were made in Scotland.

lore.title: Cast in Enniscorthy, not Stirlingshire
lore.body: Unlike most of the pillar boxes around here, which came from Carron and Company in Stirlingshire, this one was cast by Saint John's Ironworks of Enniscorthy, one of the few domestic producers of cast iron street furniture, and the works stamp is in the rear plinth. The P and T monogram is in Gaelic script and the collection information is given in Irish and English, which places it after independence.

name: Ardscoil Eanna
blurb: A house turned into a school in 1939 by Padraig Pearse's sister.

lore.title: Margaret Pearse carried on the school
lore.body: The house was converted to take a secondary school, Ardscoil Eanna, in 1939. It was set up by Margaret Pearse, sister of Padraig Pearse, together with James J. O'Byrne, continuing in a Dublin suburb the work of the Irish language school her brother had founded and which had closed after the rising of 1916.

name: Bluebell Cemetery
blurb: A church in use in 1547 and a gravestone from 1713, in an industrial estate.

lore.title: Older than everything around it
lore.body: The church on this site appears to have been in use in 1547 and the earliest known gravestone here dates from 1713. That makes this small enclosure several centuries older than the industrial and housing development that now surrounds it on every side, and it is the one piece of ground in the area that has never been built over.

name: Our Lady of Good Counsel
blurb: A 1942 church that put flat roofs and red brick where stone was expected.

lore.title: New materials on an old plan
lore.body: Built in 1942 to designs by Ashlin and Coleman. The plan and form are traditional, but the flat roofs and red brick walls were new to Irish church design at the time, which makes the building a useful marker of where architectural thinking had got to in nineteen forties Ireland. Plaques in the narthex and on the roundabout record the founding of the parish of Drimnagh in 1943.

name: Holmpatrick Church
blurb: A bell tower left from the parish church of a 13th century priory.

lore.title: Built two years after buying the estate
lore.body: The eighteenth century bell tower marks the site of the parish church of a thirteenth century Augustinian priory. The Civil Survey of 1654 to 1656 found only the walls of the parish church standing. The Hamilton family of Hackettown bought the estate from the Earls of Thomond in 1720 and built the church here two years later, which tells you what a new landlord did first.

name: Baldongan Church
blurb: A hilltop church with a carved shield of the crucifixion in the chancel.

lore.title: The shield in the chancel wall
lore.body: A national monument in a walled graveyard on a prominent hilltop, with a fifteenth century residential tower at the west end where the priest could live. The chancel is the part to look at: double arched recesses, an aumbry, dressed stone windows, and a carved shield showing the crucifixion with an altar, candles and angels. The castle that once stood beside it was removed entirely in 1975.

name: Saint Peter's Church, Balrothery
blurb: A medieval tower kept when the church beside it was pulled down in 1816.

lore.title: A head under the east window
lore.body: The church stands on what was almost certainly the footprint of the medieval parish church, which had a double aisled nave and a west tower. In 1816 the church was taken down and rebuilt with help from the Board of First Fruits, but the tower was kept and is a national monument in its own right. A carved stone head is still visible beneath an east window, and the building holds inscribed and bullaun stones.

name: Saint Movee's Chapel
blurb: Foundations in a walled graveyard sitting on a much older enclosure.

lore.title: Pottery in the wall core
lore.body: The remains sit in a walled graveyard beside a road that cuts straight through an earlier ecclesiastical enclosure, with Saint Movee's holy well close by. Only foundations survive, a small rectangle of roughly coursed masonry with a rubble core and large boulders set into the north wall. A thirteenth century pottery sherd was found inside that rubble core during a clean up in 1992.

name: Saint Maur's Chapel
blurb: A gable above Rogerstown estuary, raised by Breton sailors after a storm.

lore.title: Put up by sailors who survived
lore.body: Only the east gable still stands, with a wide pointed arched window and a modern cross set at the apex, on a rise in a graveyard overlooking Rogerstown estuary. The Civil Survey of 1654 to 1656 lists it as a chapel of ease at Whytestown. A plaque on the site records something more particular: that Breton mariners saved from a storm erected this chapel of Saint Maur.

name: Kenure Church
blurb: A church slowly being pulled apart by the graves dug up against it.

lore.title: Undermined by its own graveyard
lore.body: A plain oblong church of coursed limestone in a raised walled graveyard between Skerries and Loughshinny, with both gables still standing and a single bellcote over the west one. The east window keeps traces of fifteenth century tracery under an external hood moulding. Its trouble is structural and comes from the burials: the west gable is cracking extensively from subsidence caused by graves dug too close to it.

name: Saint Catherine's Church, Portrane
blurb: Already described as ruined in 1630, and still standing three storeys.

lore.title: Ruined for four hundred years
lore.body: A rectangular church with an undivided nave and chancel and a battlemented west tower, in a walled graveyard north of Portrane village. It was described as ruined in 1630, and the Civil Survey of 1654 to 1656 refers to the old parish church at Portrane farm, so it has stood as a ruin for the best part of four centuries. The tower rises three storeys to a belfry with Y shaped tracery.

name: Saint Doulagh's Church
blurb: A stone roof pitched at 68 degrees, said to be the steepest in Ireland.

lore.title: Duilech of Clochar
lore.body: The earliest reference to Doulagh is in the ninth century Martyrology of Oengus, where he appears as Duilech of Clochar. The east end of the church is the oldest part, from the middle of the twelfth century, and it carries a vaulted stone roof pitched at sixty eight degrees, apparently the steepest in Ireland. A chamber inside called the hermit's cell is reputed to be the founder's burial place. The central tower was added in the fifteenth century.

name: Saint Marnock's Church
blurb: The church that gave Portmarnock its name, just off Velvet Strand.

lore.title: The name is in the ruin
lore.body: The church stands off the coast road at Velvet Strand and is dedicated to Saint Marnock, whose name the town carries: Portmarnock is the port of Marnock. It was granted to Saint Mary's Abbey in 1172, and by the Civil Survey of 1654 to 1656 it was down to chapel walls. A piscina with a damaged round headed arch survives in the chancel.

name: Kinsaley Church
blurb: A ruined nave with a double bellcote, and an antiquary buried in the chancel.

lore.title: Austin Cooper lies in the chancel
lore.body: Dedicated to Saint Nicholas, the church probably fell into ruin in the middle of the seventeenth century. Only the nave remains, plain random rubble with opposed pointed segmental doorways at its west end and a tall round arched window at loft level in the west gable holding a double bellcote. The chancel arch is the only piece of the chancel left, and the tomb of the antiquary Austin Cooper stands on the chancel site.

name: Saint Brigid's Church, Stillorgan
blurb: A church of 1712 on a medieval site beside the old straight road to Shankill.

lore.title: Granted away in 1216
lore.body: A Church of Ireland building dated 1712 standing on, and partly built from, a medieval church. In 1216 Raymond de Karrue granted the church to Christ Church Cathedral, and Archbishop Luke confirmed the chapel around 1240; by 1326 the rental lists Stalorgan held by Sir Ralph the chaplain. A curving boundary wall hints at an early ecclesiastical enclosure, and the townland was crossed by what was called the greate straight road to Senekyll.

name: Carrickbrennan Church
blurb: A medieval gable built into a charnel house for storing bones.

lore.title: A gable reused for the bones
lore.body: The west gable of the medieval church of Carrickbrennan was built into a seventeenth century charnel house, the building where bones turned up by later digging were stored. The place is associated with the sixth century Saint Mochonna and was attached to the early monastery at Holmpatrick in Skerries. After the dissolution the church and its tithes passed to Sir John Travers, and Sir Edward Corker rebuilt it for the parish in 1668.

name: Kill of the Grange
blurb: A pre-Norman church with antae, founded by Saint Fintan in the 500s.

lore.title: The projecting ends give it away
lore.body: Clonkeen was founded by Saint Fintan in the sixth century and is national monument number 207. The original building was a single cell rectangle of pre-Norman date, later given a chancel to make a nave and chancel parish church with a double bellcote. It survives to gable height in coursed granite, and the antae, the wall ends that project beyond the gables in the old Irish manner, are the detail that dates it. A holy well, a bullaun and two crosses stand with it.

name: Saint Begnet's Church, Dalkey
blurb: A tall walled church in a raised graveyard right on Castle Street.

lore.title: Passed between two cathedrals
lore.body: The church sits in a rectangular walled graveyard raised above the road at the north end of Dalkey, built of coursed granite with tall nave walls and high pitched gables. Entry is through a pointed doorway in the south wall and a low lintelled doorway in the west gable. It is associated with Saint Begnet, and was assigned first to Christ Church Cathedral and afterwards to Saint Patrick's. A tomb niche and a chamfered granite stoup survive in the south wall.

name: Killiney Church
blurb: A monastery founded by a woman and her sisters in the sixth century.

lore.title: Aighleann and her sisters
lore.body: The monastery at Killiney was founded in the sixth century by its patron saint Aighleann together with her sisters, which is recorded plainly and is worth saying out loud, since most foundation stories name a man. The church ruins stand on Marino Avenue West, nave and chancel with a late medieval north aisle, the walls surviving to full height in coursed granite. A Latin cross is inscribed on the soffit of the west door lintel.

name: Tully Church
blurb: Tulach na nEpscop, the hill of the bishops, and it had eight of them.

lore.title: The hill of the bishops
lore.body: This was an early diocesan centre called Tulach na nEpscop, the hill of the bishops, and it had eight of them by the eighth century, which gives some idea of how much weight this quiet lane once carried. Brigid was its patron. The chancel survives with the footings of the nave walls, a thirteenth century chancel arch and round arched windows in which the holes for the window bars can still be seen.

name: Kiltiernan Church
blurb: A plain granite church on a south facing slope, with its font still inside.

lore.title: The font stayed put
lore.body: A plain rectangular church of granite blocks, about ten and a half metres by five and a half, standing in a walled graveyard at the top of a south facing slope. It keeps a round headed east window set in a deep embrasure, and the granite font is still in the building rather than removed to a museum. A cross incised granite slab lies outside the south east corner.

name: Garristown Windmill
blurb: A mill of 1736 standing inside an earthwork that is older than it is.

lore.title: A bank to keep the cattle off the sails
lore.body: A squat tower of randomly coursed masonry on a hilltop at 556 feet with wide views. An external plaque says Edward and Mary Walsh of Boranstown built the mill in 1736, and another stone above is marked 1827. It sits inside a circular rampart about 275 yards round which Morris described in 1939 as older than the windmill; the suggestion is that the bank was there to keep cattle away from the turning sails.

name: Skerries Five Sail Windmill
blurb: It had four sails until a fire about 1844, and came back with five.

lore.title: Rebuilt with an extra sail
lore.body: A five storey tapering tower about fifteen metres high with opposed north and south entrances, standing over Skerries. It was built as a four sail mill and became five sail and shuttered after a fire around 1844. Two pairs of grinding stones and the hoist survive with the millstones still on the spindle. A monastic lease of 1578 mentions a windmill, possibly on this same site.

name: Skerries Thatched Windmill
blurb: A tower mill capped with replica thatch, standing in an old ring fort.

lore.title: Standing in a fort on the map
lore.body: A cylindrical tower mill of four sails on a rise above Skerries, with opposed east and west entrances, now carrying a concrete capping and a replica thatched cap. The interesting detail is on the Ordnance Survey map of 1837, which draws it standing inside a circular enclosure labelled Fort, with a raised rounded bank at its base: the millwright built on top of something much older.

name: Knock Windmill Stump
blurb: A stump dated by absence, it is not on the map of 1760.

lore.title: Dated by the map it is missing from
lore.body: The Ordnance Survey map of 1837 marks a windmill stump on this eminence in Knock townland. What dates it is where it does not appear: Rocque's map of 1760 has nothing here, so the mill must belong to the later eighteenth century. The high ground is now under gorse and long grass and drops steeply away to fenced pasture below.

name: Gormanston Bridge
blurb: A 13th century bridge with one parapet built high enough to fight from.

lore.title: The high side faces upstream
lore.body: A stone bridge over the Delvin on the Dublin and Meath boundary, carrying the medieval road from Balscaddan to Gormanston and linking Dublin to Drogheda. It appears on maps of the sixteen fifties and sixties and on Rocque in 1760, and may be the oldest surviving structure on the seaboard route of the Dublin to Dunleer turnpike. The upstream parapet stands 2.1m high, probably for defence. Traffic moved to Knocknagin bridge in the late eighteenth century.

name: Naul Bridge
blurb: A crossing of the Elfin that carried the main northern road to Drogheda.

lore.title: A mill in repair, and a bridge
lore.body: The Down Survey map of 1655 to 1656 shows Paul Bridge crossing the River Elfin on the main northern route through Rathbeale and Dardistown to Drogheda. The survey terrier put it plainly: the River Elfin on which stands a mill in repair, and a bridge over the said river. A double arched bridge with round segmental arches stands on the site today.

name: Tullog Bridge
blurb: A crossing that existed before anyone built a bridge at it.

lore.title: A ford, then a mill, then a bridge
lore.body: A single arched bridge over the Delvin, forming both the Dublin and Meath county boundary and the parish boundary between Stamullin and the Naul. It served Tullog flour mill, which succeeded an earlier corn and tuck mill. Rocque's map of 1760 shows the Old Mill of Tullog and a river crossing here but draws no bridge, so people were getting across this water long before the present arch went up around 1850.

name: King William's Rampart
blurb: A boundary wall credited to two different armies forty years apart.

lore.title: Ormond's wall, William's name
lore.body: The wall forming the boundary here is called King William's Rampart, and the two halves of that name do not quite agree. It is thought to have been erected by the Duke of Ormond in 1649, but it carries the association with King William after the Battle of the Boyne in 1690. The site around it holds a holy well, the ruins of an ancient church, a graveyard and a stone high cross.

lore.title: Older than either army
lore.body: The rampart is in two sections, the northern one eighty metres long and up to three and a half metres high with a stone faced revetment and a vaulted chamber at its west end. Excavation between 1986 and 1994 produced pottery of the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries, and Office of Public Works work found fifteenth century pottery, which suggests the banks may really be a stockade protecting the manorial estate founded by Archbishop Comyn in 1181.

name: Saint Canice's Church of Ireland
blurb: Dedicated in 1843 to replace a church at the old monastery nearby.

lore.title: Dedicated by Whately
lore.body: Richard Whately, Archbishop of Dublin, dedicated this church in 1843. It was built to replace an earlier church at the nearby monastery of Saint Canice, so the congregation moved a short distance and left the older site to the graveyard and the high cross. It is a plain exercise in Commissioners' Gothic, of snecked limestone with a distinctive west gable.

name: Tolka Lodge
blurb: A lodge that first appears on the 1773 update of Rocque's survey.

lore.title: Dated by a map revision
lore.body: The lodge first appears on the 1773 update of John Rocque's survey, which is how a building with no foundation date gets one: it is absent from the earlier sheets and present on the later, so it belongs to the years between. It has canted bay windows and an elaborate Ionic doorcase, and it survives as one of the older buildings of an area otherwise rebuilt around it.

name: The Orphanage Gates
blurb: Cast iron gates that are all that is left of an orphanage for 150 boys.

lore.title: The gates outlasted the institution
lore.body: These cast iron gates survive from Saint Vincent de Paul's Male Orphanage, which has been demolished. The Christian Brothers established it and it opened about 1860 for a hundred and fifty boys, to designs by John Sterling Butler, with extensions in the eighteen nineties. The institution has gone entirely; the way in and out of it is still standing on the street.

name: North Road Milestone
blurb: A marker on the old coach road out towards Slane and Ardee.

lore.title: On the Slane coach road
lore.body: The North Road was the coach road linking Dublin with Slane and Ardee, and it is drawn as such in Taylor and Skinner's Maps of the Roads of Ireland, compiled in 1777. The milestone is a relic of that traffic. A road now running through north city suburbs was, within the life of this stone, the way out of Dublin towards the midlands.

name: Jessop Davis Postbox
blurb: A postbox with a Celtic Revival monogram, cast in County Wexford.

lore.title: Cast by a foundry that lasted seventy years
lore.body: The box carries a Celtic Revival P and T motif and was cast by the Jessop Davis Foundry of Enniscorthy in County Wexford, a works that operated from about 1890 to 1964. Most Irish pillar boxes came from Scottish foundries, so a domestically cast one carrying deliberately Gaelic lettering is a small piece of economic and political history bolted to a footpath.

name: Sunnybank
blurb: Birthplace of a press baron, and a house that turns up in Finnegans Wake.

lore.title: Northcliffe was born here
lore.body: One of several well built houses put up on the edge of Chapelizod in the nineteenth century, backing onto Martin's Row and fronting the Liffey inside a high rubble stone wall. It was the birthplace of the newspaper man Alfred Harmsworth, Lord Northcliffe, who founded the Daily Mail. The house, along with several of its neighbours, is mentioned in James Joyce's Finnegans Wake.

name: Chapelizod Weir
blurb: You see the weir by the shape of the water rather than the stone.

lore.title: Older than the map that first shows it
lore.body: The weir appears on the six inch first edition Ordnance Survey map surveyed in 1837, and it may well be older than that record. The structure itself is not clearly visible; what you see is the water it makes, still above the curve and gentle rapids below. It is a reminder that Chapelizod was an industrial village, one of a series of such structures along the Liffey.

name: Saint Laurence's Church, Chapelizod
blurb: The reputed site of Isolde's chapel, which is where the village name comes from.

lore.title: Isolde's chapel
lore.body: The church and its setting are the reputed site of Isolde's Chapel, from which Chapelizod takes its name. A medieval tower stands with a nave of the mid nineteenth century by Frederick Darley and a later Gothic vestry by Welland and Gillespie; unusually, the chancel was not added until 1908. The churchyard is the one named in Sheridan Le Fanu's ghost story The House by the Churchyard.

name: Royal Hospital West Gate Lodge
blurb: A small lodge marking a west entrance that once had two sets of gates.

lore.title: Two gates, not one
lore.body: This modest lodge marked the west entrance to the Royal Hospital Kilmainham and was an integral part of that complex. The detail worth noticing is the gate pier standing to the west of it, which shows that there was originally a second set of gates at this point, and therefore more security on the way in than a single lodge and gate would suggest.

name: Bremore Passage Tomb
blurb: The best of five mounds at the Delvin mouth, quarried for sea defences.

lore.title: Taken for coastal defences
lore.body: A grassed circular cairn twenty nine metres across and three and a half high at the mouth of the river Delvin, the best preserved of the five mounds of the Bremore cemetery. Disturbance on the north west suggests a collapsed passage and chamber. It was reportedly damaged in the nineteen forties when the Board of Works extracted stone from it to build coastal defences, so a tomb of the fourth millennium went into a wall against invasion.

name: Bremore Castle
blurb: A Barnewall manor with triple diamond chimney stacks, rebuilt from a ruin.

lore.title: Six hundred acres and an attorney general
lore.body: The manor castle of Bri Mhor, held by the Barnewall family from the fourteenth century; James Barnewall was appointed Attorney General in 1559 and the estate ran to six hundred acres, with manorial privileges granted in 1669. The late sixteenth or early seventeenth century fabric shows the characteristic triple diamond chimney stacks and mullioned windows. The upper floors were rebuilt in the twentieth century by the Fingal County Council parks department.

name: Saint Molaga's Church
blurb: A manorial chapel on a monastic site called Lann Beachaire.

lore.title: A lintel dated 1689
lore.body: A late medieval manorial chapel in a disused graveyard south of Bremore castle, standing on the reputed early monastic site of Lann Beachaire, possibly founded by Saint Molaga in the seventh century. The building is a plain rectangle of coursed limestone with an undivided nave and chancel. Decorated seventeenth century stonework survives, including a lintel dated 1689 carved with the emblems of the Passion.

name: Newhaven Pier
blurb: A sixty metre dry stone pier that was already disused by the 1830s.

lore.title: A harbour that fell out of use
lore.body: A substantial dry stone pier about sixty two metres long on the southern side of Bremore headland, below a sixteenth century settlement. It is drawn on the Down Survey maps of 1655 to 1656 and on eighteenth century mapping, but by the time of the first Ordnance Survey it was no longer in use. The pier averages eight to ten metres wide and there is a possible mooring stone midway along it with a hole through the centre.

name: Saint Finian's Well
blurb: A well said to have flooded the village after soldiers fouled it in 1798.

lore.title: The well that took revenge
lore.body: An enclosed natural spring dedicated to Saint Finian, described in 1937 folklore as about three feet across and two feet high with a concrete coping. The story attached to it is specific: that in 1798 English soldiers desecrated the well and it flooded the village in response, the waters only receding when the curate blessed it. The same tradition records a lame man who bathed his foot in the water for three weeks and recovered.

name: Saint Bridget's Well
blurb: A well for sore eyes, still collecting rags and coins from visitors.

lore.title: Rags, rosary beads, coins and pencils
lore.body: A spring enclosed by railings, a stone wall and a small stone roofed chamber, marked by a mature ash tree and dedicated to Brigid. It is said never to run dry. People came for eye ailments, bathing the eyes with the water, and returning more than once. A school account of 1937 lists what was left behind at the site: bits of rags, bits of rosary beads, old coins and pencils.

name: Annesley Icehouse
blurb: The only thing left of a 1790s house, and it was the part for storing ice.

lore.title: The service building outlived the house
lore.body: The icehouse is the only physical remnant of Annesley Lodge, which John Sutherland designed for Richard Annesley in the seventeen nineties and which was later known as Clare Grove. It is heavily overgrown but keeps its original form and traces of earlier render. Big houses needed ice all year for the kitchen, and what survives here is the plumbing of an estate rather than the estate itself.

name: Knocknagin Harbour
blurb: A harbour of about 1760 partly built from a robbed passage tomb.

lore.title: A boat load of large fillers
lore.body: The harbour was built around 1760 and is drawn on the Ordnance Survey map of 1837. Two farm diary entries give away where the stone came from: one of 1806 records moving a very large stone from the mound at Newhaven, and one of 1818 a boat load of large fillers brought from Newhaven. The mound in question is the passage tomb cemetery along the headland.

name: Cloich Choirneal Standing Stone
blurb: A standing stone on an estate green, with plough scars on its lower face.

lore.title: Ploughed around for centuries
lore.body: A four sided stone a metre and a half high standing on landscaped open space in a housing estate, which took its name from the stone rather than the other way round. The detail to look for is low on the west face: plough marks, cut by generations of farmers who worked right up to the stone and went round it rather than remove it. A flower bed was set around its base in 2010.

name: The Howe Stone
blurb: A lichened stone on a crest with long views, known locally as the Howe.

lore.title: The Ho, or the Howe
lore.body: A single lichen covered stone a little over a metre high on the crest of high ground with extensive views around it. It is traditionally known as the Ho or Howe stone. A dump of stones has gathered round its base and the ground level has crept up around it through intensive agriculture, so it stands lower now than it once did.

name: Stewart's Hospital
blurb: An institution that used Coade stone, an artificial stone with a lost recipe.

lore.title: Coade stone, and how it was lost
lore.body: An imposing building in the landscape, and its noteworthy material is Coade stone. Coade was an artificial stone made in Lambeth from the seventeen sixties, harder wearing than most natural stone, and the recipe was closely held by the firm and effectively lost when it closed. Finding it this far from London on a nineteenth century institutional building is unusual enough to be worth the detour.

name: Palmerstown Graveyard
blurb: Ground in religious use since the seventeenth century, unbroken since.

lore.title: Four hundred years of the same use
lore.body: The site has been in religious use since the seventeenth century, which makes it a valuable social and historical document for the area: the one piece of Palmerstown that has been doing the same thing continuously since before the village around it existed in its present form. The headstones record the families of a place that has otherwise been rebuilt entirely.

name: Spawell House
blurb: The house at the spa well that gave this whole corner its name.

lore.title: There really was a spa well
lore.body: A large house characteristic of the early eighteenth century, and of historical note for where it stands rather than how it looks: it sits at the original spa well, and the City Watercourse runs close by to the north. The name Spawell attached to a roundabout, a leisure complex and a road in this part of Templeogue starts with the spring this house was built beside.

name: Cypress Grove House
blurb: Built by a Mr Paine for a Sir William Cooper, and still has its doorway.

lore.title: Named builder, named client
lore.body: A substantial Georgian former country house built by Mr Paine for Sir William Cooper. It is unusual for a suburban house of this date to carry both names, since most Georgian houses around Dublin have lost the record of who actually built them and survive only with the name of the family who lived there. It keeps much original fabric, including an impressive doorway.

name: Templeogue Graveyard
blurb: A church ruin and old headstones marooned beside a busy junction.

lore.title: An old site kept by a new road
lore.body: A good ecclesiastical group with a long history of occupation, holding many fine headstones and the picturesque ruin of the church. What makes it worth stopping for is its position: it sits prominently beside a busy modern junction, so a site that has been in use for centuries is now an island in the middle of twentieth century road engineering.

name: Peamount House
blurb: A Palladian country house that became the centrepiece of a hospital.

lore.title: A country seat turned sanatorium
lore.body: A handsome, substantial former Palladian country house which is no longer in domestic use but keeps its imposing form and some internal features. It now acts as the focal point of the hospital grounds that grew up around it, which is what happened to a good many houses of this kind in the early twentieth century when institutions needed large buildings in clean air.

name: The Manor Farmhouse
blurb: The farm that fed the hospital, then held its library, then its staff.

lore.title: Three jobs in one building
lore.body: A handsome former farm house with a history tied closely to Peamount House and the hospital beside it. The farm supplied food for the hospital, so the institution grew much of what it ate on its own ground. When that stopped the building was turned over to use as a library, and later again to accommodation for the workers.

name: Saint Finian's Corrugated Iron Church
blurb: A church built of corrugated iron, and still in regular use.

lore.title: A tin church that lasted
lore.body: A distinctive and unusual church that shows an increasingly rare vernacular use of corrugated iron as a building material. Tin churches were put up quickly and cheaply and were meant as a stopgap until something permanent could be afforded, which is exactly why so few survive. This one is still in regular use and gives the hospital grounds much of their character.

name: Saggart Mill Pond
blurb: A mill pond that outlived its mill and became a wildlife habitat.

lore.title: Water kept for a wheel that has gone
lore.body: This picturesque body of water is a former mill pond, held back to guarantee a supply to a water wheel no matter what the stream was doing. The mill it served has gone and the pond has stayed, and it is now a valuable habitat for local wildlife. It is one of the clearest reminders that Saggart was a milling village.

name: Glenaraneen Mill Ponds
blurb: A mill pond now fished, left behind when the water wheel was replaced.

lore.title: Outlasted the change of power
lore.body: The surviving mill pond is now in use as a fishing lake. It was built to serve a water wheel driven mill at Saggart, and it became redundant in two stages: first when the mill changed its source of power away from water, and then when the mill closed altogether. The pond was the one part of the works worth keeping.

name: Saggart Graveyard
blurb: In use since the 1890s, with a handsome gate and carved headstones.

lore.title: A village reading itself in stone
lore.body: The graveyard has been in use since the eighteen nineties and holds many finely carved headstones behind a handsome entrance gate. For a village of this size it is the single most important social and religious focus, and the stones between them record most of the families who have lived and worked in Saggart across the last century and a quarter.

name: Olympia Theatre
blurb: Ireland's first film screening happened here in 1896, in a music hall.

lore.title: Star of Erin to Olympia
lore.body: The Star of Erin Music Hall was established here behind an eighteenth century house in 1879, built for Dan Lowrey to designs by J.J. O'Callaghan with its main entrance from Crampton Court. In 1896 it was the location of the first screening of a cinematic film in Ireland. Richard Henry Brunton remodelled it completely into the Empire Palace Theatre of Varieties in 1897, and it was renamed the Olympia in 1923 after independence.

name: Dublin City Walls
blurb: A tenth century bank of earth and timber, then the wall that tripled the town.

lore.title: The wall that tripled the town
lore.body: Dublin's first defences were tenth century: an ovoid enclosure of earth and timber on the ridge above the meeting of the Poddle and the Liffey, with a bank four metres high and a timber palisade. Around 1015 the town pushed west and the first Hiberno-Norse stone wall replaced the earthworks in massive limestone blocks, nearly tripling the defended area. Significant stretches of it survive along Cook Street.

name: The Lion Rampant House
blurb: A corner house with a lion on a tablet, from a walled town most forget.

lore.title: Chapelizod had a wall and a gate
lore.body: The medieval town of Chapelizod was surrounded by a wall which was still standing at the beginning of the seventeenth century, and an eastern gate is recorded. This two storey square house at the corner of Saint Martin's Row may belong to that town: it has a chamfered first floor corner with traces of moulding, and on the north face a tablet carrying a lion rampant above moulding that once held a motto.

name: Saint Patrick's Island Monastery
blurb: Raided by Vikings in 798, and they broke the shrine of the founder.

lore.title: Burning of Inis Patraice by Gentiles
lore.body: An early Christian monastery on Inis Phadraig, linked to the seventh century Saint Mochonna and venerated on the thirteenth of January. The Annals of Ulster record the raid of 798 in four words: burning of Inis Patraice by Gentiles, adding that the shrine of Dochonna was broken by them. That is among the earliest recorded Viking attacks on Ireland. Aerial photography shows a roughly circular enclosure around the church.

name: The Ordnance Survey Ha-Ha
blurb: A sunken wall around the oval enclosure of a park keeper's house.

lore.title: Gardiner's oval in the park
lore.body: The walls, gateway and sunken ha-ha here form the boundary of an oval enclosure around the former house of Luke Gardiner, a Keeper of the Park who also developed much of the Georgian north inner city. A ha-ha is a wall set in a ditch so it keeps stock out without interrupting the view. The site was assigned for use as a cavalry barracks about 1780.

name: Mountjoy House
blurb: Built as Castleknock Lodge, the oldest building on the Ordnance Survey site.

lore.title: A villa that became a map office
lore.body: The earliest building on the site, put up as Castleknock Lodge, the suburban villa of Luke Gardiner. It was built in stages and Edward Lovett Pearce may have had a hand in it. Its early to mid eighteenth century interior is well documented. A private house in a deer park became the headquarters from which the whole country was mapped, which is a considerable change of purpose.

name: The Fireproof Map Store
blurb: A building designed to be fireproof, because it held the maps.
