lore.title: The one thing you cannot replace
lore.body: A purpose built map store designed by J. Howard Pentland on the site of an earlier outbuilding to Mountjoy House. The requirement that shaped it was simple: it was designed to be fire proof. The survey's maps were the accumulated work of decades of field measurement and could not be redone quickly, so the building that held them was constructed around the risk of losing them.

name: Phoenix Park School
blurb: A school built inside the park for the park workers' children.

lore.title: Part of Decimus Burton's park
lore.body: The school was built as part of the wider improvements to Phoenix Park carried out by Decimus Burton, and it was for a specific group of children: those of the employees of the Commissioners of Woods and Forests. Enough people worked in and lived on the park that it needed its own school inside the walls rather than sending the children out to the city.

name: Phoenix Park Worker's House
blurb: A picturesque estate cottage for the men who ran the park.

lore.title: Designed, not thrown up
lore.body: The house was built to designs by Enoch Trevor Owen, who was responsible for a number of fine buildings within Phoenix Park. It is worth noticing that a house for a park employee was given to a named architect rather than put up to a standard pattern, which says something about how the park was run and how much its appearance mattered to the Commissioners.

name: The Ballast Office Wall
blurb: Two stone walls built in 1759 with the gap between them packed with sand.

lore.title: A wall with sand for a middle
lore.body: In 1759 the Ballast Office built a double stone wall at Ringsend, and the method is the interesting part: two walls were run parallel between eleven and fourteen metres apart and the space between them was filled with sand. An earlier attempt in 1715 had piled the south side of the channel below Ringsend with three rows of braced piles, sheeted with woven wattle hurdle and packed with shingle and stone.

name: Binns Bridge
blurb: Named for a canal backer, with the credit carved on both faces.

lore.title: Beaten by the railway that bought it
lore.body: The bridge is named for John Binns, one of the principal supporters of the Royal Canal, and its construction is commemorated in a carved stone plaque on each face. The canal was developed in the later eighteenth century to carry freight and passengers between Dublin and the Shannon. In the middle of the nineteenth century the Midland Great Western Railway bought it outright, and in the eighteen sixties ran a branch line to North Wall along this very stretch.

name: Saint Edmondsbury Icehouse
blurb: An icehouse pinned to a twenty six year window by two map editions.

lore.title: Dated between two surveys
lore.body: An icehouse in woodland forty metres east of the Liffey, belonging to the demesne of Saint Edmondsbury House a little over a hundred metres to the south east. Its date comes from the mapping rather than from any document: it is absent from the six inch Ordnance Survey edition of 1837 and drawn as a circular structure on the twenty five inch maps of 1863, so it was built in the years between.

name: Woodlands Icehouse
blurb: A rectangular icehouse in woodland, set beside its own spring well.

lore.title: Built beside the water it needed
lore.body: Marked as Ice House on the Ordnance Survey six inch map of 1837 and drawn as a rectangle, standing in woodland on the demesne of Woodlands House. The siting is deliberate: there is a watercourse and a spring well close by. Ice was cut in winter, packed in the chamber and drawn on through the year, and having water and shade to hand was what made that possible.

name: The Phoenix Park Wall
blurb: Eleven miles of wall built in 1662, and the mason was paid under protest.

lore.title: A row about the stonework, settled in 1665
lore.body: The crown seized the lands of the Priory of Kilmainham north of the Liffey early in the seventeenth century to make a royal deer park, and began walling it in 1662. The mason Henry Gamble worked on it in 1664 and 1665 and there was a dispute over his workmanship and his money. A survey of 1665 found the wall well and in workmanlike manner performed, blaming the defects on soft stones laid without mortar rather than on him.

name: The Salute Battery
blurb: Twelve cannon on the highest ground in the park, fired on rejoicing days.

lore.title: Given away for a monument
lore.body: A description of 1818 puts it neatly: the Salute Battery, situated on the highest ground in the Park, mounting twelve pieces of cannon, twelve pounders, which are fired on rejoicing days. It appears on Taylor's map of 1816 and partly hachured on the Ordnance Survey of 1837. The Board of Ordnance then handed the site to the Wellington Committee, and the monument was built partly on top of the battery.

name: Pigeon House Fort
blurb: A fort out on the South Wall that had a prison and a handball alley.

lore.title: Quarters, magazines and a handball alley
lore.body: Established as a military post on the South Wall shortly before 1798, and it was a small town in itself: soldiers' quarters, stores, magazines, a hospital, a canteen, a handball alley, a prison, water tanks, defensive gateways, an armoury and a guardhouse. A description of 1835 says the wall runs in a straight line into the sea the astonishing length of 17,754 feet. The fort declined once Howth and Dun Laoghaire harbours were built.

name: The Half Moon Battery
blurb: A five gun battery on the South Wall that became a swimming place.

lore.title: From guns to swimmers
lore.body: Built in the middle seventeen nineties on the South Wall about eight hundred metres short of Poolbeg lighthouse, and armed with five twenty four pounder guns commanding the river channel. An addition was made in 1795. The battery was later dismantled and the site was taken over for a quite different purpose: it became a swimming place, and the name Half Moon stayed with the water rather than the guns.

name: Dalkey Island Battery
blurb: Three gun emplacements and a shot furnace for a garrison of twelve.

lore.title: Overlapping fields of fire
lore.body: Battery number nine sits at the south end of Dalkey Island with three gun emplacements facing north, east and south across Dalkey Sound, armed with five twenty four pounders. It held a shot furnace for heating cannonballs and quarters for a garrison of twelve soldiers. Built from 1804 and finished by December 1805, its fire was directed southwards over Killiney Bay so as to overlap with the batteries either side.

name: Saint Mobhi's Holy Well
blurb: A well inside a horseshoe of boulders, with a bullaun set in the wall.

lore.title: The font that refills itself
lore.body: Reached by a footpath at the gate lodge to Milverton Hall, inside an ecclesiastical enclosure traced by geophysical survey, a little over a hundred metres from the medieval church of Saint Mobhi's monastery. The well is enclosed by an impressive horseshoe shaped cairn of large boulders with steps down on the east, and a bullaun is set into its north wall. Folklore calls that bullaun a hollow stone like a holy water font whose curative water mysteriously refills.

name: Tibradden Cairn
blurb: A Bronze Age cairn with a passage, a cist and a food vessel inside.

lore.title: A cross carved on the boulder below
lore.body: A Bronze Age cairn on the north west slopes of Tibradden Mountain, with a central cist in a circular chamber about three metres across that held a bowl food vessel and a cremation, and a partly lintelled passage running north east from it. A secondary urn burial was found inside as well. A granite boulder thirty metres to the south east carries an incised cross and figure decoration. It has been under preservation order since 1940.

name: Windmill Hill
blurb: A windmill built into the southern quadrant of a prehistoric cairn.

lore.title: Found by lidar in 2014
lore.body: A broad low circular cairn forty metres across and a metre and a half high sits on the summit, commanding extensive views, and it was only identified from lidar analysis in 2014. A windmill occupies its southern quadrant, so the millwright built into a burial monument without apparently recognising it. The cairn sits off centre inside a further enclosure following the contours of the ridge, possibly a hillfort.

name: Piperstown Hill
blurb: A hillside of small cairns, pits and cremations above Glenasmole.

lore.title: Six standing stones round a pit
lore.body: Site K on the south slopes of Piperstown Hill looked like an irregular low cairn, under four metres across and half a metre high, before it was excavated. Six orthostats marked out its perimeter and a circular pit at the centre held charcoal and cremated bone with a flint flake. It is one part of an extensive Late Neolithic and Early Bronze Age settlement and cemetery spread across this hillside.

name: Ballymadrough Graveyard
blurb: A raised oval burial ground above Malahide estuary, closed to burials.

lore.title: A member of parliament for Swords
lore.body: A raised oval platform immediately north of Malahide estuary, twenty seven metres by twenty two and up to nearly two metres high, enclosed now by a modern wall that appears to have replaced an earlier earthen bank. A sunken rectangle towards the west end is probably the church. According to the local historian Peadar Bates the gravestone here is that of William Massey, who died in 1777 and was member of parliament for Swords.

name: Kilcrea Graveyard
blurb: An overgrown graveyard by the estuary, reached across a drainage ditch.

lore.title: Walled in the 1990s, then left
lore.body: A graveyard by the roadside near Malahide estuary holding a plain rectangular church of which the east gable and side walls still stand. A modern concrete wall was put round it in the early nineteen nineties, forty five metres by thirty, and it is entered through an opening in the east wall across a drainage ditch. It is no longer used for burial and is extremely overgrown.

name: Malahide Demesne Graveyard
blurb: A small graveyard behind a battlemented wall in the castle grounds.

lore.title: Burials found half a metre down
lore.body: A small sub circular graveyard in the castle grounds opposite the renovated courtyard, enclosed by a battlemented wall about forty metres by forty five and a curving hedgerow, holding inscribed gravestones of the eighteenth to twentieth centuries and loose architectural fragments. Monitoring during redevelopment found skeletal remains half a metre down, laid east to west and cut through by modern service trenches.

name: Brackenstown Canal
blurb: Recorded as a fish pond, it is really a 1714 canal thirty yards broad.

lore.title: A Whig's idea of a garden
lore.body: Two broad undulating banks topped with trees run across this ground, and the survey first recorded them as a fish pond. They are in fact a canal, cut between 1714 and 1719 as part of Robert Molesworth's landscape design and described at the time as thirty yards broad and flanked double on each side by two walks, with trees planted along them. It reflects Whig philosophy and Italianate design, and it held fish as well.

name: Swords Mill
blurb: A corn mill drawn in 1655, painted about 1790, photographed about 1900.

lore.title: Three pictures of the same wheel
lore.body: The Down Survey map of 1655 to 1656 shows a mill at the north end of Swords village, and the early Ordnance Survey six inch mapping probably marks the same corn mill. A painting of about 1790 by George Holmes shows the mill wheel south of the bridge, which the maps call Mill Bridge, and photographs of the wheel and the weir from about 1900 are in the National Library. The millrace runs along the west side of Swords Castle.

name: Saint Laurence O'Toole School
blurb: A modernist school dropped into the north docks in the 1930s.

lore.title: An exciting new style in the 1930s
lore.body: The school was designed by the architectural practice of Robinson and Keefe in what was, in the nineteen thirties, an exciting new style. Modernism arrived in Irish public building through schools and hospitals rather than through houses, so a functional flat fronted school in a nineteenth century dockland street is one of the places where the change of architectural direction is easiest to see on the ground.
